title: About
text:
ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications introduces the concepts, principles and methods of geospatial analytics and their application to real-world problems — from spatial point pattern analysis and measures of spatial autocorrelation through to geographically weighted regression, accessibility modelling and spatial interaction models.
The course emphasises four things:

Performing geospatial data science tasks programmatically — importing, tidying, transforming, projecting and processing geospatial data.
Visualising and describing geographical patterns with appropriate geovisualisation and thematic mapping techniques.
Conducting analysis with appropriate spatial statistics and geospatial machine learning methods.
Communicating the entire pipeline in a reproducible report.

Built with Quarto, version-controlled on GitHub, and deployed continuously. Each exercise page documents the analytical choices made, not just the code that ran — including, where relevant, what the result would have looked like had a different choice been made.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
This exercise has three parts.
Part 1 covers the data preparation: importing vector data from several sources, getting their coordinate reference systems to agree, converting a table of coordinates into a spatial object, and answering two questions using geoprocessing.
Part 2 joins population data to the subzone boundaries and maps it as a choropleth. Most of the work there is about choosing a classification scheme rather than accepting the default.
Part 3 goes beyond what the chapters ask for. I wanted to check how much the conclusions depend on the classification I picked, whether the pattern holds when the spatial units change, and whether bringing in a second dataset could explain the pattern instead of just describing it.






NoteReference



r4gdsa Chapter 1 — Geospatial Data Science with R and Chapter 2 — Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation with R.








NoteAnselin’s four types of spatial data



The pre-lesson lecture by Luc Anselin, “Spatial Data, Spatial Analysis, Spatial Data Science”, sets out four types of spatial data. Three of them show up in this exercise:








Anselin’s type
In this exercise
Note




Points
Pre-schools, Airbnb listings
He separates points that are events (crimes, accidents) from points that are locations of objects (stores, facilities). Ours are the second kind


Lattice / areal units
Subzone polygons
His term for administrative zones. Relevant later, since MAUP is a lattice problem


Networks
Cycling paths
Nodes and links. Treated as plain lines here. Network-constrained analysis comes in Lesson 7


Surfaces
not used
Continuous fields needing interpolation, like air quality or price surfaces



He also names the standard that the sf package implements: the Simple Features specification from the Open Geospatial Consortium. That is where the name “sf” comes from, and why every function starts with st_ (spatial type).
He also poses the problem that §“How many pre-schools are in each subzone?” solves below: “You look at the map, you know immediately that city is in that county. How would a computer know that that point is inside that polygon?” In R, the answer is st_intersects().








NoteXie et al. on the three foundations



The second pre-lesson reading, Xie et al. (2017), “Transdisciplinary Foundations of Geospatial Data Science”, argues that every geospatial technique rests on three foundations, and that problems arise when any of them is treated as a black box. All three appear in this exercise:








Foundation
Their concern
Where it appears below




Mathematics
Geometry, topology, projection
The CRS transform to EPSG:3414, and st_intersects() as a topological predicate rather than a lookup


Statistics
Spatial data violate the i.i.d. assumption most methods rely on
The correlation in Part 3, and the caveat attached to it


Computer science
Efficiency, scalability, filter-and-refine
st_intersects() builds a spatial index instead of testing 323 × 2,290 pairs



One warning from the paper is useful throughout: “traditional density-based clustering methods will generally output chance patterns if applied to geospatial hotspot detection”. K-means will find clusters in pure noise, so finding a pattern is not by itself evidence that one exists. Anselin makes the same point with his shuffled map.

4.3 Working with projection

st_crs(mpsz14)$input

[1] "WGS 84"

st_crs(cyclingpath)$input

[1] "WGS 84"

st_crs(preschool)$input

[1] "WGS 84"


All three arrived as WGS84 (EPSG:4326), a geographic CRS whose units are degrees, which is not usable for anything involving distance or area. A one-degree buffer would be roughly 111 km, and near the equator a degree of longitude and a degree of latitude are not the same distance on the ground anyway.
Singapore’s national projected CRS is SVY21, EPSG:3414, and its units are metres.

mpsz14      <- st_transform(mpsz14, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool   <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

st_bbox(mpsz14)

     xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
 2667.538 15748.721 56396.440 50256.334 


The bounding box now shows six-figure easting and northing values instead of degrees, so the transform worked.






ImportantDifference between st_set_crs() and st_transform()



These two are easy to confuse and I want to be able to state the difference precisely.
st_set_crs() changes the label on the coordinates without touching the numbers. It asserts that the numbers were always in that system. It should only be used when the data arrived with a missing or wrong CRS tag and you know what the correct one is.
st_transform() changes the numbers, recalculating every coordinate into the target system. It is what you use when you actually need the data in a different CRS.
Using the wrong one produces no error and no warning. You just get a layer sitting off the coast of Africa, or distances wrong by a factor of 100,000, and nothing downstream will flag it.

4.4 Trying the KML version
When a classmate asked on Piazza whether GeoJSON was acceptable given that data.gov.sg no longer serves KML, Prof Kam replied: “It is fine. However, there is nothing wrong to explore the kml very. You will learn more by trying.”
So I tried it. Writing one layer out to KML and reading it straight back shows what the format costs.

dir.create("data/geospatial/kml", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

st_write(mpsz14,
         "data/geospatial/kml/MP14_Subzone.kml",
         driver = "KML",
         delete_dsn = TRUE,
         quiet = TRUE)

mpsz14_kml <- st_read("data/geospatial/kml/MP14_Subzone.kml", quiet = TRUE)


tibble(
  aspect = c("Number of attribute columns", "Column names", "CRS", "Feature count"),
  geojson = c(as.character(ncol(mpsz14) - 1),
              paste(head(setdiff(names(mpsz14), "geometry"), 4), collapse = ", "),
              st_crs(mpsz14)$input,
              as.character(nrow(mpsz14))),
  kml = c(as.character(ncol(mpsz14_kml) - 1),
          paste(head(setdiff(names(mpsz14_kml), "geometry"), 4), collapse = ", "),
          st_crs(mpsz14_kml)$input,
          as.character(nrow(mpsz14_kml)))
) %>%
  kable(caption = "What survives a round trip through KML")

ImportantWhat changed after the KML round trip



The attribute table collapsed. All the named columns, SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N and the rest, were flattened into a generic Name field and a Description field containing an HTML fragment. The geometry came back intact but the schema did not. To analyse the result I would have to parse the attributes back out of HTML strings, which is the same state the Pre-Schools GeoJSON arrives in.
The CRS reverted to WGS84. The KML specification requires WGS84, so st_write() reprojected out of the SVY21 metres I had just transformed into, without warning me. Reading it back gives degrees again, and every buffer and area calculation in this document would be wrong until I transformed it a second time.
This does not mean KML is bad, just that it is a presentation format, designed for drawing things in Google Earth where a person reads the description bubble. GeoJSON and shapefile are analysis formats that keep typed attribute columns and let you declare a projected CRS. The chapter’s instruction to use shapefile or KML predates data.gov.sg switching to GeoJSON, and for this work GeoJSON is the best of the three.

4.6 Geoprocessing

4.6.1 How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?
This is a buffer and area problem. The scenario is that LTA wants to know how much land would be needed to widen the entire cycling network by 5 m on each side.

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)
buffer_cycling$AREA <- st_area(buffer_cycling)
sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

4989654 [m^2]



total_ha <- sum(buffer_cycling$AREA) %>% units::set_units("hectares")
total_ha

498.9654 [hectares]








NoteNotes on this figure



The units are carried by the object. st_area() returns a units object, so sum() reports m² explicitly and set_units() converts safely. Whether the 5 meant five metres or five degrees is exactly what the earlier transform to EPSG:3414 settled. In WGS84 this buffer would have been about 555 km wide.
This total double-counts the overlaps. Where two cycling paths run close together their buffers intersect, and summing the per-feature areas counts that shared land twice. For a land acquisition estimate the buffers should be dissolved first:

dissolved_ha <- buffer_cycling %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_area() %>%
  units::set_units("hectares")

dissolved_ha

431.5118 [hectares]


The difference between the two figures is the overlapping area, and it is not small. Reporting the first number as a land requirement would overstate it.



overlap_pct <- as.numeric((total_ha - dissolved_ha) / total_ha * 100)
sprintf("Naive sum overstates the true footprint by %.1f%%", overlap_pct)

[1] "Naive sum overstates the true footprint by 13.5%"

5.1.1 Every count column arrived as text

All 61 columns came in as character, including the population counts. The cause is one token: SingStat writes suppressed or zero cells as -, and that forces readr to type the whole column as text.






WarningWhy the columns imported as text



rowSums() on character columns errors immediately, which is the lucky outcome. The version that would have caused real trouble is code that coerces silently and returns a wrong number that looks plausible.

5.2 Computing the dependency ratio
The age dependency ratio is the number of people not usually in the labour force, meaning children under 15 and adults 65 and over, per person of working age.
\[\text{Dependency} = \frac{\text{population}_{0-14} + \text{population}_{65+}}{\text{population}_{15-64}}\]

young_cols  <- c("Total_0_4", "Total_5_9", "Total_10_14")
active_cols <- c("Total_15_19","Total_20_24","Total_25_29","Total_30_34","Total_35_39",
                 "Total_40_44","Total_45_49","Total_50_54","Total_55_59","Total_60_64")
aged_cols   <- c("Total_65_69","Total_70_74","Total_75_79","Total_80_84",
                 "Total_85_89","Total_90andOver")

popdata_sz <- popdata %>%
  filter(Number != "Total",
         !str_detect(Number, " - Total$")) %>%
  mutate(
    SUBZONE_N = toupper(str_trim(Number)),
    YOUNG     = rowSums(across(all_of(young_cols))),
    ACTIVE    = rowSums(across(all_of(active_cols))),
    AGED      = rowSums(across(all_of(aged_cols))),
    TOTAL     = Total_Total,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / ACTIVE
  ) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, YOUNG, ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY)

5.6 Classification methods
tmap supports the standard data classification schemes. They are not just style options. Each one makes a different claim about what the reader should be noticing.

make_map <- function(style, title) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = style, n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
                col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title(title, size = 0.9)
}

tmap_arrange(
  make_map("equal",    "equal — equal value ranges"),
  make_map("quantile", "quantile — equal counts"),
  make_map("jenks",    "jenks — natural breaks"),
  make_map("sd",       "sd — deviation from mean"),
  ncol = 2
)














ImportantComparing the four classification methods



These are four maps of the same numbers.
Equal interval cuts the value range into equal-width bins. On a skewed variable this pushes almost everything into the lowest class and the map ends up looking empty.
Quantile puts an equal count of subzones into each class. It always produces a visually balanced map, including when there is no real variation to show, which is the risk with it.
Jenks minimises within-class variance and finds breaks at natural gaps in the distribution. It is usually the most faithful to the structure, but the breaks depend on the data, so two maps made this way cannot be compared to each other.
Standard deviation shows distance from the mean. It answers a different question, which areas are unusual rather than how much there is.

ImportantThe effect of one outlier



The maximum dependency ratio is 9.5 against a median of 0.45, so roughly twenty times the typical value. It is not a data error. It is a subzone with very few residents where the age mix happens to be extreme, and the small denominator produces a very large ratio.
Equal-interval and standard-deviation both derive their breaks from the range, so that one subzone stretches the whole scale and every other subzone falls into the first class. Quantile and Jenks derive their breaks from the ordering and the distribution instead, so they are not affected.
The practical rule is that range-based classification fails on a variable with outliers. You either use a rank or distribution based scheme, or handle the outlier explicitly and say which you did.




5.6.2 How much does the choice actually change?
Rather than just assert that classification matters, I wanted to measure it. How many subzones actually change class when the scheme changes?

vals <- mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY[!is.na(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY)]

  brks <- classIntervals(vals, n = 5, style = s)$brks
  as.integer(cut(vals, breaks = unique(brks), include.lowest = TRUE))
})
colnames(class_assign) <- styles

pairs <- combn(styles, 2, simplify = FALSE)
sens <- map_dfr(pairs, function(p) {
  changed <- mean(class_assign[, p[1]] != class_assign[, p[2]], na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  tibble(comparison = paste(p[1], "vs", p[2]),
         pct_subzones_changing_class = round(changed, 1))
}) %>% arrange(desc(pct_subzones_changing_class))

Someone who saw only the equal-interval map and someone who saw only the quantile map would describe Singapore’s dependency geography differently, and neither would have any reason to know it.
For this variable I would use Jenks for exploration, since it respects the actual distribution, and quantile only when comparing across time periods, where fixed relative positions matter more than absolute breaks. Equal interval should not be used on a right-skewed variable at all.

tmap_arrange(
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.greens"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE), col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title("Sequential (greens)", size = 0.9),
  tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5,
                                                values = "-brewer.greens"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE), col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_title("Reversed — misleading here", size = 0.9),
  ncol = 2
)














NoteChoosing sequential or diverging



A sequential palette says the variable runs from less to more with no meaningful midpoint. A diverging palette says there is a midpoint that matters, and that deviations on either side of it differ in kind rather than degree.
For a dependency ratio a diverging scheme can be justified if the midpoint is chosen for a reason, such as the national ratio, because being above or below the national average really are different situations. It cannot be justified if the midpoint is just the middle of the data range, since that invents a threshold that does not exist.
The reversed map above shows what goes wrong. Dark now reads as low dependency, which inverts the intuition most readers bring to a map. The code is correct and the communication is not.

6.1 Is this actually spatial analysis?
Anselin proposes a test for whether an analysis is genuinely spatial:

“If you change the location of things and it doesn’t matter, then it’s not spatial analysis. But if it does matter, then it is.”

He demonstrates it with two maps of Milwaukee, one real and one with the same values randomly shuffled between census tracts. The histograms are identical but the maps look like two different cities.
I wanted to run the same test on this data rather than take it on faith.

set.seed(1234)

mpsz_shuffled <- mpsz_pop
mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY <- sample(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY)

Every value is preserved, since sample() only reassigns which subzone holds which number. So any non-spatial summary should come out exactly the same:

  sd      = c(sd(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), sd(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE)),
  median  = c(median(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), median(mpsz_shuffled$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE))
) %>%

shuffle_map <- function(dat, ttl) {

    tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5,

The mean, standard deviation and median are identical, and so is the histogram. But the two maps look nothing alike. The real one has coherent regions of similar colour and the shuffled one is more or less visual static.
Everything separating those two images is spatial structure, and none of the conventional statistics can detect it. This seems to be the gap the rest of the course fills. Lesson 4’s spatial weights formalise what neighbouring means, and Lesson 5’s Moran’s I turns the difference between these two maps into a single number with a significance test.
It also answers a question I had at the start, which was why not just use pandas for this. A non-spatial toolkit would report these two datasets as identical, because on every measure it can compute, they are.

6.2 Does the pattern survive a change of spatial unit? (MAUP)
The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem is that statistical results change when the zoning or the scale of the spatial units changes. It applies to most of what this course covers, and it can be tested directly here because subzones nest inside planning areas.

mpsz_pa <- mpsz_pop %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL)) %>%
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) %>%
  summarise(YOUNG = sum(YOUNG), ACTIVE = sum(ACTIVE), AGED = sum(AGED),
            n_subzones = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(DEPENDENCY_PA = (YOUNG + AGED) / ACTIVE) %>%
  filter(is.finite(DEPENDENCY_PA))

comparison <- tibble(
  unit = c("Subzone", "Planning area"),
  n = c(sum(is.finite(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY)), nrow(mpsz_pa)),
  min = c(min(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), min(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA)),
  median = c(median(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), median(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA)),
  max = c(max(mpsz_pop$DEPENDENCY, na.rm = TRUE), max(mpsz_pa$DEPENDENCY_PA))
) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))

       subtitle = "Same population, same ratio definition, different spatial units",
       x = "Dependency ratio", y = "Density", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()








The planning-area distribution is noticeably narrower. Aggregating averages away the extremes, so a map drawn at planning-area level would understate how uneven dependency actually is across Singapore. Neither scale is the correct one. The best I can do is state which scale I used and note that the result depends on it.






NoteThe two components of MAUP



Anselin separates MAUP into two distinct problems:

The scale problem. Results change with the size of the unit, which is what the table above measures, moving from subzone up to planning area.
The zoning problem. Results change with the arrangement of the units even when their size stays constant. Redrawing the boundaries into equally sized but differently shaped subzones would move the answer again.

The standard demonstration is Openshaw’s “A Million Spatial Autocorrelation Coefficients”, which recomputed the same statistic on Iowa election data across progressively larger units and found that the magnitude changed and so did the sign.
Only the scale problem can be tested here, because Singapore’s subzones nest inside planning areas and there is no alternative zoning available. I am noting that rather than implying the test covered both.








WarningChange of support



This is Anselin’s term for combining data recorded on units that do not align. This document has a mild case of it, since Part 1 uses Master Plan 2014 boundaries and Part 2 uses 2019, which is what the chapters specify. Subzone definitions changed between the two versions, so the pre-school counts and the dependency ratios are not measured on quite the same geography.
Because of that, the cross-dataset section below recalculates pre-school counts against the 2019 boundaries instead of reusing the numbers from Part 1.

6.3 The choropleth’s built-in bias
A choropleth encodes a rate using area. The eye reads area as quantity, so large sparsely populated subzones dominate the map while the dense subzones where most people actually live barely register.

    `Share of map area held by the least-populated half of subzones (%)` =
      round(sum(area_km2[TOTAL <= median(TOTAL)]) / sum(area_km2) * 100, 1),
    `Share of population they hold (%)` =
      round(sum(TOTAL[TOTAL <= median(TOTAL)]) / sum(TOTAL) * 100, 1)
  ) %>%

6.4 Does provision follow need? Joining two datasets
Everything up to this point describes the data. This section is an attempt to explain something, by asking whether pre-school provision tracks the child population. It brings the pre-school data from Part 1 together with the demographics from Part 2.

preschool_by_sz <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = toupper(SUBZONE_N),
         PreSch_Count = lengths(st_intersects(., preschool))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PreSch_Count)

provision <- mpsz_pop %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(TOTAL), YOUNG > 0) %>%
  left_join(preschool_by_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(children_per_preschool = YOUNG / pmax(PreSch_Count, 1),
         has_none = PreSch_Count == 0)

nrow(provision)

[1] 230



ggplot(provision, aes(x = YOUNG, y = PreSch_Count)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = has_none), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#4A6FA5", "TRUE" = "#D1495B"),
                     labels = c("has pre-schools", "none"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Pre-school provision broadly tracks child population",
       subtitle = "Each point is a subzone; red points have resident children but no pre-school",
       x = "Residents aged 0-14", y = "Pre-schools in subzone") +
  theme_minimal()









ct <- cor.test(provision$YOUNG, provision$PreSch_Count, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
sprintf("Spearman rho = %.3f (p = %.3g), n = %d",
        ct$estimate, ct$p.value, nrow(provision))

[1] "Spearman rho = 0.855 (p = 5.42e-67), n = 230"








WarningWhy the p-value here is not reliable



Spearman’s ρ treats the 230 subzones as independent observations, and they are not. Adjacent subzones have similar child populations for the same underlying reasons, such as housing type, estate age and planning policy, so the observations are spatially autocorrelated.
Xie et al. describe this as the central statistical issue in the field: “Geospatial data are often spatially auto-correlated, which violates the i.i.d. assumption of many data mining and machine learning techniques.”
What this means in practice is that the effective sample size is smaller than 230, because neighbouring subzones carry partly redundant information. The correlation coefficient is still fine as a description. The p-value is not, because it is anti-conservative, meaning too small, and the significance is overstated by an amount I cannot quantify.
So I am reading ρ = 0.86 as a strong association and ignoring the p-value rather than reporting it as if the test were valid. Doing this properly needs a method that models the spatial dependence, which is what Lessons 4 and 5 introduce, and presumably why they come before the regression lessons.
Xie et al. add a second point that applies here, which is that a p-value alone is never enough to rule out a chance pattern and should be paired with an effect size.

  arrange(desc(YOUNG)) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, YOUNG, TOTAL) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(caption = "Subzones with the most children but no pre-school within their boundary")

ImportantLimits of this finding



The correlation is strong and positive, so provision does broadly follow population. The table then does something the correlation cannot, which is name specific subzones where children live and no pre-school falls inside the boundary.
That is a starting point rather than a conclusion, for four reasons:

The denominator problem. Anselin’s car theft example applies here: “wouldn’t there be more car thefts where there are more cars?” A raw count of pre-schools mostly tells you where the children are, not where provision is good or bad. I framed this against child population instead of using a bare count for that reason, and the earlier density section divided by area rather than mapping counts for the same reason.
Edge effects. A subzone boundary is not a catchment area. A pre-school 50 m outside the line still serves those children. Doing this properly would involve buffering, or computing distance to the nearest facility, rather than counting inside polygons, which is the accessibility modelling covered in Lesson 9.
Capacity is not measured. Counting facilities treats a 30-place centre and a 300-place centre as the same thing.
The demographic data is from Census 2020 while the pre-school locations are current. A six-year gap matters in a country that builds new towns as quickly as Singapore does.

So this identifies candidates worth investigating, and the right next step would be a distance-based accessibility measure rather than a count.
Xie et al. make the point that a false positive is not a neutral error, using the example of a community “being incorrectly identified as a cancer cluster”. Naming a subzone as underserved is a much smaller version of the same thing, but it still directs attention and possibly resources, so I have listed these caveats here rather than leaving them out.








WarningEcological fallacy



Anselin describes this as the classic trap in aggregate spatial work: “confusing individual behaviour with aggregate behaviour… the mistake happens at the end, when the conclusions are written as if they are about individual behaviour, but really they’re based on aggregate magnitudes.”
Everything above is measured on subzones rather than on families, so these statements would not be supported by this data:

✗ “Families in these subzones cannot find pre-school places.”
✗ “Children here are less likely to attend pre-school.”

What the data does support:

✓ “These subzones have resident children and no pre-school within their boundary.”
✓ “Across subzones, pre-school count rises with child population (ρ = 0.86).”

The gap between those two lists is the ecological fallacy. As Anselin puts it, an aggregate only represents individuals well when the individuals are alike. A subzone containing both high and low income households has an average that describes nobody living in it.

6.5 Limitations

Two boundary vintages. Part 1 uses Master Plan 2014 and Part 2 uses 2019, since that is what the chapters specify. Subzone definitions changed between the two, so figures are not strictly comparable across the two parts.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
This exercise applies Spatial Point Patterns Analysis (SPPA) to the locations of childcare centres in Singapore. It follows the two chapters assigned for Lesson 2: r4gdsa Chapter 4 and Chapter 5. Where I write “the chapters” below, I mean those two.
Part 1 reproduces the first-order methods from r4gdsa Chapter 4: methods that measure the intensity of points: the Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour index and kernel density estimation, including bandwidth selection, kernel choice, and fixed versus adaptive bandwidth.
Part 2 reproduces the second-order methods from Chapter 5: methods that measure the spatial dependence between points: the G, F, K and L functions, each tested against Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) using Monte Carlo envelopes, for two contrasting planning areas.
Part 3 is where most of my time went. It is a working diary: the choices the chapters leave to the software, how far the conclusions move when those choices change, what the week’s readings add when applied to this data, and where the analysis runs out.

3.3 Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test
Clark and Evans (1954) compare the mean observed nearest-neighbour distance against what would be expected under Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR). The index R is the ratio of the two:

R < 1: points are closer than random, so clustered
R ≈ 1: consistent with CSR
R > 1: points are further apart than random, so regular/dispersed


clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = sg_owin,
                alternative = "clustered")

    No edge correction
    Z-test

alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


The test can also be run as a Monte Carlo simulation rather than the analytic normal approximation, which is slower but does not rely on distributional assumptions.

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,

                clipregion = sg_owin,
                alternative = "clustered",
                method = "MonteCarlo",

    No edge correction

3.4 Kernel density estimation
The Clark–Evans index collapses the whole pattern into one number. KDE keeps the geography: it spreads a kernel over each point and sums the surfaces, producing a continuous density field that shows where intensity is high and low.

3.4.1 Automatic bandwidth selection
The bandwidth (the sigma of the kernel) controls how far each point’s influence extends, and it drives the appearance of the result more than anything else in KDE. The package offers several automatic selectors; the default is bw.diggle.

kde_SG_diggle <- density(childcareSG_ppp,
                         sigma = bw.diggle,

3.4.2 Comparing the selectors
The four common selectors optimise different criteria, so they return different bandwidths. Rather than accept the default silently, I compare them.

4.543204 



bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

There is an order-of-magnitude spread here, from about 0.39 km (bw.ppl) to 4.54 km (bw.CvL). Since all four are defensible choices, the map itself is only as settled as the selector behind it. Part 3 works through what that does to the surface.
bw.scott stands out here, because it is the rule Donthu and Rust use. They pick the bandwidth that would be optimal if the data were bivariate normal, while admitting “we have no reason to actually expect the underlying distribution to be bivariate normal”. On this data that rule returns about 2.2 km against bw.diggle’s 0.30 km, roughly seven times wider. Since their paper uses the density surface to choose a store location, the two rules would suggest visibly different catchments from identical data. The 1989 advice is not wrong, but it is much smoother than a modern cross-validation selector, and a siting decision taken from one surface rather than the other would land in a different place.


3.4.3 The kernel function
The kernel is the shape of the influence region. spatstat’s default is Gaussian; quartic and Epanechnikov kernels are common alternatives. At the same bandwidth they produce broadly similar surfaces, differing mostly in how sharply the tails fall off.

A fixed bandwidth applies the same smoothing radius everywhere. An adaptive bandwidth shrinks the radius where points are dense and widens it where they are sparse, which is usually the better assumption for a service like childcare whose supply follows population density closely.

kde_ab <- adaptive.density(childcareSG_ppp_km, method = "kernel")


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

plot(kde_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
5.1 Reviewing the chapters’ choices

5.1.1 Checking for coincident points
This check belongs before any of the distance methods run. Baddeley, Rubak and Turner (2015), listed in the Lesson 2 references and written by the authors of spatstat, set out why in section 3.4.4:

Duplication of points is important, because statistical methodology for spatial point processes (as used in this book) is based largely on assumption that processes are simple, i.e. that points of the process can never be coincident. When the data have coincident points, some statistical procedures designed for simple point processes will be severely affected. For example, the pair correlation function will have an infinite value at distance zero. It is strongly advisable to check for duplicated points and to decide on a strategy for dealing with them if they are present.

Coincident points are plausible for this data, since several childcare centres can operate in the same mall or HDB block and geocoding would return one coordinate for all of them. So it is worth running the check.

c(points = npoints(childcareSG_ppp),
  unique_locations = npoints(unique(childcareSG_ppp)),
  duplicated = sum(duplicated(childcareSG_ppp)),
  nn_distances_of_zero = sum(nndist(childcareSG_ppp) == 0))

              points     unique_locations           duplicated 
                1925                 1925                    0 
nn_distances_of_zero 
                 338 


This layer is clean: every centre has its own coordinate, no nearest-neighbour distance is zero, and the pair correlation function used later in Part 3 is safe to run. Nothing needs fixing here, but that is only knowable after running the check.
It is worth knowing what a failure here would look like, because I met one. An earlier draft of this exercise used a different geocoded childcare file, CHILDCARE.shp, distributed with a later chapter of the same book. That version had 174 duplicated coordinates, including one location carrying 25 centres, and it changed results: the Clark-Evans index read 0.495 instead of 0.494, and the adaptive-bandwidth surface in Part 1 peaked at 314 centres per square kilometre instead of about 47, because an adaptive kernel shrinks its bandwidth wherever intensity is high and a 25-point stack drives that bandwidth towards zero. The resulting map was almost entirely dark, since the colour ramp stretched to a maximum reached by a dozen pixels. Fixed-bandwidth KDE was unaffected, because it spreads every point over the same radius regardless of how many neighbours it has.


5.1.2 A clipregion argument that does nothing
A smaller one. The chapter calls the Clark-Evans test like this:
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp, correction = "none",
                clipregion = "sg_owin", alternative = c("clustered"))
clipregion is passed the string "sg_owin" rather than the object sg_owin. It reads as though the test is being clipped to the Singapore boundary. It is not: the argument is only used by the guard-area correction, and with correction = "none" it is ignored entirely. Passing the object, passing the string, or omitting the argument all return R = 0.49444. The line is harmless but misleading, and I dropped the quotes in Part 1.


5.1.3 The envelopes are pointwise, and one argument does not exist
Chapter 5 builds the K and L envelopes like this:
K_ck.csr <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Kest, nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)
glocal is not an argument of envelope(). The argument that controls this behaviour is called global, so glocal = TRUE is absorbed by ..., passed down to Kest, and ignored. The envelopes come out pointwise, which is the default, and identical to what you get by leaving the argument out.

set.seed(1)
e_default <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(1)
e_glocal  <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, glocal = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(1)
e_global  <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp, Lest, nsim = 99, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

c(glocal_same_as_default = identical(e_glocal$hi, e_default$hi),
  global_same_as_default = identical(e_global$hi, e_default$hi))

glocal_same_as_default global_same_as_default 
                  TRUE                  FALSE 


The distinction matters, and it is the difference between two questions.
A pointwise envelope is built separately at each distance r. At any single r it has the stated error rate, but the plot shows hundreds of distances at once, so the chance that the observed curve strays outside somewhere is far higher than the nominal level. Reading a pointwise band as though a single excursion proves clustering is the multiple-comparison problem in graphical form.
A global envelope is built from the largest deviation each simulated curve reaches anywhere in the range, so the band is wider and one excursion anywhere is enough to reject at the stated level.

i <- round(length(e_default$r) / 2)
data.frame(
  envelope = c("pointwise", "global"),
  lo = round(c(e_default$lo[i], e_global$lo[i]), 1),
  hi = round(c(e_default$hi[i], e_global$hi[i]), 1),
  frac_r_outside = round(c(mean(e_default$obs > e_default$hi | e_default$obs < e_default$lo),
                           mean(e_global$obs  > e_global$hi  | e_global$obs  < e_global$lo)), 3)
)

   envelope    lo    hi frac_r_outside
1 pointwise 359.8 447.9          0.431
2    global 333.8 458.0          0.010


For Choa Chu Kang’s L function the pointwise band puts about 43% of the distance range outside the envelope, and the global band about 1%. Same data, same simulations, different question.
Because of this I report the second-order results below as a yes-or-no answer under a global envelope, rather than as a percentage of the range under a pointwise one. The percentage is useful for describing where along the distance axis a departure sits, but it is not a significance level and should not be read as one.
One practical detail: the pair correlation function is undefined at r = 0 and returns Inf there, which a global envelope will always flag. Every test below is evaluated over r > 0 with non-finite values dropped.


5.1.4 Choosing the study window
Every first-order and second-order statistic is computed inside a window, so the window you choose changes the numbers you get. Three things I noticed:

The national window follows the coastline. as.owin(sg_boundary) produces an irregular polygon. The nearest-neighbour distances near the coast are truncated by the boundary, which biases R upward (points appear more dispersed than they are) unless an edge correction is applied. clarkevans.test with correction = "none" makes no allowance for this.
The national Clark–Evans index answers a question I did not mean to ask. R = 0.49 confirms clustering, but childcare supply follows population, and population in Singapore is itself clustered. A nearest-neighbour test against uniform CSR asks the wrong question when the points track an underlying covariate. The same weakness affects the second-order tests in Part 2.
The window changes how strong the result looks. Clark-Evans compares the observed mean nearest-neighbour distance with the distance expected under CSR, and that expected distance depends on the area of the window through the intensity n/A. Enlarge the window without adding points and CSR expects the points to be further apart, so the same points look more clustered by comparison.
The test below holds the 74 Choa Chu Kang centres fixed and only changes the window.


ck_pts <- childcare_ck_ppp
windows <- list(
  `planning-area polygon` = as.owin(st_union(ck)),
  `polygon + 500 m buffer` = as.owin(st_buffer(st_union(ck), 500)),
  `convex hull of points`  = convexhull.xy(ck_pts$x, ck_pts$y),
  `bounding box`           = owin(range(ck_pts$x), range(ck_pts$y))
)
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(windows), function(nm) {
  w <- windows[[nm]]
  Y <- suppressWarnings(ppp(ck_pts$x, ck_pts$y, window = w))
  t <- suppressWarnings(clarkevans.test(Y, correction = "none",
                                        alternative = "two.sided", nsim = 999))
  data.frame(window = nm, area_km2 = round(spatstat.geom::area(w) / 1e6, 2),
             R = round(unname(t$statistic), 3), p = round(t$p.value, 3))
}))

                  window area_km2     R     p
1  planning-area polygon     6.12 0.841 0.009
2 polygon + 500 m buffer    12.60 0.586 0.000
3  convex hull of points     5.79 0.865 0.026
4           bounding box     9.03 0.692 0.000


All four windows agree that the pattern is clustered, which is reassuring, but they do not agree on how strongly. R ranges from 0.87 under the convex hull to 0.59 under the buffered polygon, and the p-value moves from 0.026 to below 0.001. Nothing changed but the outline I drew around the same 74 centres. A result reported as “R = 0.87, p = 0.03” and one reported as “R = 0.59, p < 0.001” would be written up quite differently, even though they describe the same centres. Wartman and Malasavage’s insistence that “the study area should be determined objectively, rather than arbitrarily” is doing real work here, and neither chapter mentions the issue.
O’Sullivan and Unwin explain the mechanism behind the buffered case: edge effects arise because “sites in the center of the study area can have nearby observations in all directions, whereas sites at the edges only have neighbors toward the center”. Padding the window adds empty space full of edge, which is why R falls furthest there.
Two of the applied papers sit usefully side by side here. Borruso and Porceddu write that the bandwidth “represents the only arbitrary variable which defines the extent of the searching function”, while Wartman and Malasavage insist that “the study area should be determined objectively, rather than arbitrarily”. Borruso’s sentence is about the KDE kernel, so the table above is not a counter-example to it. But his paper never treats the study area as a choice at all, and on this data the study area is what moved the verdict, with no bandwidth involved. Following Borruso alone, an analyst would carefully document the one parameter he names and say nothing about the one that mattered.


5.1.5 How much the bandwidth choice matters
Yin (2020), one of the week’s core readings, frames KDE as a bias-variance trade-off: too small a bandwidth produces a noisy surface that overfits the sample, too large a bandwidth smooths away the structure we are looking for. The four automatic selectors sit at different points on that trade-off, and on this data they are far apart.








Selector
Bandwidth (km)
What it optimises




bw.diggle
0.30
Edge-corrected minimisation of mean-square error (the book’s default)


bw.ppl
0.39
Likelihood cross-validation, driven by the data rather than a formula


bw.scott
2.16 / 1.40 (x / y)
A rule of thumb based on the pattern’s own spread


bw.CvL
4.54
Coarser smoothing, low variance, high bias



The spread is more than tenfold. Since the chapters pick one without saying why, the question is how much of the map depends on that choice, so I re-ran the national surface under the two extremes alongside the default.

kde_ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = bw.ppl, edge = TRUE)
kde_cvl <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = bw.CvL, edge = TRUE)


par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")
plot(kde_cvl, main = "bw.CvL")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The broad pattern is stable across all three: the same dense central-east corridor, the same relative voids in the north. What changes is the granularity. The two small bandwidths break the surface into many separate peaks, while bw.CvL merges them into a few large blobs. So the statement “childcare is concentrated in the central and eastern regions” is robust, but any claim about a particular hotspot is a claim about the bandwidth as much as about the data.
The trade-off can also be measured. The coefficient of variation of the density values says how uneven each surface is.

cv_im <- function(x) { v <- as.vector(x$v); v <- v[!is.na(v)]; sd(v) / mean(v) }
c(`bw.ppl` = cv_im(kde_ppl), `bw.diggle` = cv_im(kde_childcareSG_km), `bw.CvL` = cv_im(kde_cvl))

   bw.ppl bw.diggle    bw.CvL 
1.5432064 1.6760748 0.6119746 


The ordering follows the bandwidths rather than the reputations of the methods. bw.diggle returns the smallest bandwidth here at 0.30 km and gives the most uneven surface, bw.ppl at 0.39 km is close behind, and bw.CvL at 4.54 km is far smoother than either. The book’s default therefore sits at the variance-heavy end of the range on this data rather than in the middle, which is the opposite of what I assumed before measuring it.


5.1.6 A unit mismatch in the KDE map
The chapters build the KDE map by rescaling the point pattern to kilometres, converting the result to a raster, and then assigning the raster the CRS EPSG:3414, which is a metre projection. The raster’s extent (about 0–55 in km units) is then interpreted by tmap as 0–55 metres. The rendered map is a sliver of the coastline about fifty metres wide, not the country, even though the density surface is correct.
The fix used for the KDE map in Part 1 is to compute the density on the metre-based pattern, so the raster extent is genuinely in metres and the CRS assignment is honest, then rescale only the values by 10⁶ for a per-km² legend. The change is small, and the map then shows Singapore properly.
What makes this one instructive is that nothing failed. The code ran without error and produced a map that looked reasonable at a glance. I only caught it by reading the graticule labels, which spanned about a hundredth of a degree.


5.1.7 Why adaptive suits this data
The default density() uses a fixed bandwidth: every point spreads its influence to the same radius. Adaptive bandwidth (adaptive.density) lets the radius shrink where points are dense. For childcare, whose supply tracks population density, adaptive is the more defensible assumption: a centre in a dense town competes with neighbours close by, while one in a sparse area stands alone.
In the comparison plotted in Part 1, the fixed surface smooths the dense corridor into one continuous mass while the adaptive surface keeps more local structure. Which one is preferable depends on what you are asking, so the choice should be stated explicitly.


5.1.8 Do the functions agree?
All four functions describe the same underlying dependence from different angles, so reading them against each other is a way of checking that a result is not an artefact of one particular statistic:

G and K/L both detect clustering in both planning areas, with the observed curves sitting above the CSR band at short distances.
F rarely leaves its band. F is computed from arbitrary locations, so it reflects the average empty-space structure. With only 74 and 117 points in these two areas, F is blunt; it contributes little beyond confirming there is no large-scale regularity.
K and L give the cleaner contrast between the two towns. G looks only at each point’s nearest neighbour and is sensitive to the border correction, while K and L average over all pairs. That stability comes from accumulating counts across distances, which is an advantage here and a liability later: the section on nulls below shows the same accumulation producing a signal that turns out not to be there.



5.1.9 Why the two towns differ
Both towns show clustering at short distances, but Tampines is more strongly clustered, with its K/L curves rising higher above the band.
The likely explanation is the housing. Tampines is one of the earliest and densest new towns, built around a tight commercial centre with residential blocks close by, while Choa Chu Kang is younger and more spread out. Childcare centres locate near homes, so the arrangement of the centres largely follows the arrangement of the flats. That explanation comes from knowing the towns, not from the curves.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
5.2 Applying the week’s material
I have already used two of the readings above: Yin (2020) for the bandwidth comparison, and Yuan et al. (2020) for the argument that CSR is the wrong null when points follow population. The two methods below come from material outside r4gdsa Chapters 4 and 5. Quadrat analysis is covered in the Lesson 2 slides and in Anselin’s Point Pattern Analysis: Quadrat Counts. The inhomogeneous null then tests Yuan’s warning, which is that CSR treats every location as equally likely to hold a centre, so any service that follows the population will be reported as clustered whether or not the centres have anything to do with each other.

5.2.1 Quadrat analysis
Neither r4gdsa Chapter 4 nor Chapter 5 covers quadrat analysis, but the Lesson 2 slides and Anselin’s Point Pattern Analysis: Quadrat Counts both do, so I have added it here as a third first-order method. It is the oldest of them. You divide the study area into a grid, count the points in each cell, and compare those counts with what CSR would produce. Quadrat analysis adds a different kind of evidence from Clark-Evans, which measures distances between centres. Quadrat analysis ignores distance entirely and looks only at how counts vary between cells, so if the two agree, the finding does not depend on either way of measuring.

qc <- quadratcount(childcareSG_ppp_km, nx = 6, ny = 6)

The slides give the reading rule through the variance-mean ratio. Under CSR the counts follow a Poisson distribution, whose variance equals its mean, so VMR ≈ 1 is random, VMR > 1 is clustered and VMR < 1 is regular.

counts <- as.vector(qc)
c(variance = var(counts), mean = mean(counts), VMR = var(counts) / mean(counts))

  variance       mean        VMR 
8885.09032   62.09677  143.08457 



quadrat.test(childcareSG_ppp_km, nx = 6, ny = 6)


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcareSG_ppp_km
X2 = 1388.7, df = 30, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 31 tiles (irregular windows)


The chi-square test is unambiguous: X² = 1389 on 30 degrees of freedom, p < 2.2e-16, the same strong clustering Clark-Evans found. The raw VMR of 143 is also far above 1, but it is inflated and should not be reported on its own. The count grid inherits the coastline, so several edge tiles straddle land and sea and sit near zero, while the busiest central tile holds 277 centres.
This is the one method in the exercise where the modifiable areal unit problem applies in its strict sense, because it is the only one that aggregates points into areal units before computing anything. O’Sullivan and Unwin describe MAUP as the problem that “the aggregation units used are arbitrary with respect to the phenomena under investigation, yet the units used will affect statistics determined on the basis of data reported in this way”.
A 6 by 6 grid is exactly such an arbitrary unit. Change nx and ny, or shift the grid origin, and the counts, the VMR and the chi-square statistic all move. That sensitivity, which the Lesson 2 slides list among the weaknesses of quadrat analysis, is why the field moved to distance-based methods.
So quadrat analysis agrees with Clark-Evans that the pattern is clustered, which is reassuring, but its headline number depends on a grid I chose arbitrarily. That dependence is the reason later methods measure distances between points instead of counts inside cells.


5.2.2 Two functions the chapters leave out
r4gdsa Chapters 4 and 5 stop at G, F, K and L. Two of the other references go further, and both additions turned out to matter.
Anselin’s Point Pattern Analysis: F and J Functions introduces the J function, which combines the two curves already computed: J(r) = (1 - G(r)) / (1 - F(r)). Under CSR it is flat at 1, below 1 means clustering and above 1 means inhibition. It is a tidier answer to the question I asked earlier about whether G and F agree, since it combines them arithmetically instead of leaving me to compare two plots by eye.
Chapter 11 Point Pattern Analysis of Intro to GIS and Spatial Analysis, listed in the references, makes a second point. K and L are cumulative: they count every point within distance r, so clustering at short range keeps inflating the curve at longer ranges. The pair correlation function counts only points in a narrow band at r, so each distance is judged on its own.






WarningTwo different functions, one letter



The pair correlation function is written lowercase g(r), and it is not the G-function from the lesson slides and Chapter 5. They are unrelated:

G(r), Gest(), is the cumulative distribution of nearest-neighbour distances, so it uses one distance per point and says nothing about what lies further away.
g(r), pcf(), is derived from Ripley’s K by differentiating it, so it uses all pairs of points and reports the density of pairs at each separation.

Gimond introduces g in section 11.3.3 as a modification of K, not of G, which is the clearest way to keep them apart. To avoid the collision in code I have named the objects pcf_* rather than g_*, since Part 2 already uses G_ck and G_tm for the G-function.



childcare_tm_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")

set.seed(42)
J_tm <- envelope(childcare_tm_ppp_km, Jest, nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
pcf_tm <- envelope(childcare_tm_ppp_km, pcf,  nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
J_ck <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp_km, Jest, nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
pcf_ck <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp_km, pcf,  nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(J_tm, main = "J function: Tampines", legend = FALSE)
plot(pcf_tm, main = "Pair correlation g: Tampines", legend = FALSE)







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


outside <- function(env, side = c("above", "below")) {
  side <- match.arg(side)
  if (side == "above") mean(env$obs > env$hi, na.rm = TRUE)
  else mean(env$obs < env$lo, na.rm = TRUE)
}
data.frame(
  town        = c("Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang"),
  J_clustered = c(outside(J_tm, "below"), outside(J_ck, "below")),
  g_clustered = c(outside(pcf_tm, "above"), outside(pcf_ck, "above"))
)

           town J_clustered g_clustered
1      Tampines   0.7704918  0.98437500
2 Choa Chu Kang   0.2042254  0.06835938


Those percentages are pointwise, so they describe where along the distance axis each curve leaves its band, not whether the departure is significant overall. The section on envelopes above explains why. Repeating both tests under a global envelope, over r > 0, gives the answer that can actually be reported:

exits <- function(e) {
  k <- is.finite(e$obs) & e$r > 0
  any(e$obs[k] > e$hi[k] | e$obs[k] < e$lo[k], na.rm = TRUE)
}
glob <- function(X, fun, ...) { set.seed(42)
  envelope(X, fun, nsim = 99, global = TRUE, verbose = FALSE, ...) }

data.frame(
  town = c("Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang"),
  J_global   = c(exits(glob(childcare_tm_ppp_km, Jest)),
                 exits(glob(childcare_ck_ppp_km, Jest))),
  pcf_global = c(exits(glob(childcare_tm_ppp_km, pcf)),
                 exits(glob(childcare_ck_ppp_km, pcf)))
)

           town J_global pcf_global
1      Tampines    FALSE       TRUE
2 Choa Chu Kang    FALSE       TRUE


The two functions part company. The pair correlation function rejects CSR for both towns under the stricter test, so the clustering it reports is not an artefact of scanning many distances. The J function does not reject for either town, even though its pointwise band was left over 77% of the range in Tampines. J is built from G and F, both of which are cumulative nearest-neighbour constructions, and its deviations are correspondingly small and spread out rather than concentrated. Under a band sized for the whole curve, they no longer stand out.
So on the CSR comparison I would report the pair correlation result and treat the J result as suggestive only. Under CSR, Tampines is clustered on both pointwise measures, with J outside its band over about 77% of the range and g over 98%, while Choa Chu Kang is much weaker at roughly 20% and 7%.
Clark-Evans reports both towns as significantly clustered, at R = 0.67 for Tampines and R = 0.84 for Choa Chu Kang, and stops there. What the distance-resolved functions add is that the two are clustered in different ways. Tampines departs from randomness at nearly every distance, while Choa Chu Kang does so only over a narrow band. A single nearest-neighbour index cannot express that difference, because it collapses the whole pattern into one number before distance enters the picture.
The non-cumulative view matters again in the next section, where it changes a conclusion I had already written down.


5.2.3 Choosing a null hypothesis
Everything in Part 2 was tested against Complete Spatial Randomness, which assumes a centre was equally likely to open anywhere in the town. For a service that follows families, that assumption is close to guaranteed to report clustering. This section builds two better nulls and then sets out what neither of them can settle.

5.2.3.1 A null estimated from the pattern itself
Yuan et al. (2020) warn that CSR is a weak null for events that track covariates. The warning is testable directly. The homogeneous L-function in Part 2 compares the observed pattern with a completely random one, which is loaded here: if childcare follows population density, the intensity gradient is counted as clustering. The inhomogeneous L-function removes the trend first. It estimates the intensity (here, the KDE surface) and tests the pattern against an inhomogeneous Poisson process with that intensity, so any clustering that survives is interaction between points that the trend cannot explain.

set.seed(42)   # envelope simulations are random; fix the seed so the results are reproducible
lambda_tm <- density(childcare_tm_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
lambda_tm$v <- pmax(lambda_tm$v, 0.01)   # Linhom needs strictly positive intensity
L_tm_inhom <- envelope(childcare_tm_ppp_km, Linhom, lambda = lambda_tm,
                       nsim = 99, correction = "Ripley")

A coarse summary of where the observed curve sits relative to the envelope makes the difference easy to read.

frac_band <- function(env) c(above = mean(env$obs > env$hi, na.rm = TRUE),
                            below = mean(env$obs < env$lo, na.rm = TRUE))
list(Tampines = frac_band(L_tm_inhom),
     `Choa Chu Kang` = frac_band(L_ck_inhom))

$Tampines
    above     below 
0.0000000 0.9259259 

$`Choa Chu Kang`
      above       below 
0.003898635 0.625730994 


Under the homogeneous test, both towns look strongly clustered. Under the inhomogeneous null the picture changes, and the two towns differ. For Tampines the observed curve sits below the envelope for most of the plotted range (about 92% of it), which is the signature of regularity, not clustering: once the density of centres is accounted for, centres are further apart than the trend predicts. For Choa Chu Kang the curve hovers at or below the envelope (about 49% of the range below it, essentially none above), so the clustering the homogeneous test reported for this town was almost entirely the intensity trend, with no clear residual signal left.
Both results line up with Yuan’s warning: a homogeneous null will overstate clustering for any service that follows population.
The Tampines curve sitting below the envelope looks like regularity, and my first reading of it was that centres compete and space themselves out. That reading was wrong, and the pair correlation function from the previous section is what shows it. L is cumulative, so a small deviation repeated across short distances accumulates into a curve that drifts below the band without any single distance being unusual. Running the same null through the non-cumulative pcfinhom removes that accumulation.

set.seed(42)
pcfi_tm <- envelope(childcare_tm_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lambda_tm,
                  nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
pcfi_ck <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lambda_ck,
                  nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(pcfi_tm, main = "Inhomogeneous g: Tampines", legend = FALSE)
plot(pcfi_ck, main = "Inhomogeneous g: Choa Chu Kang", legend = FALSE)







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


data.frame(
  town = c("Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang"),
  g_inhom_outside_envelope = c(outside(pcfi_tm, "above") + outside(pcfi_tm, "below"),
                               outside(pcfi_ck, "above") + outside(pcfi_ck, "below"))
)

           town g_inhom_outside_envelope
1      Tampines                        0
2 Choa Chu Kang                        0


The inhomogeneous g never leaves its envelope for either town at any distance. So the regularity I thought I had found was an artefact of L accumulating, not a property of the centres. Once the intensity trend is accounted for, there is no detectable interaction between childcare centres at any distance.
The direction of the correction is worth being clear about. A global band is wider, which makes it harder to reject the null and easier to stay inside. So for a result that rejects, like the pair correlation test above, the global version is the stricter test. For a result that finds nothing, like this one, the narrower pointwise band was already the harder test to pass, and the global check below is a formality. I ran it so both conclusions are reported on the same footing.

data.frame(
  town = c("Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang"),
  pcfinhom_global_exits = c(exits(glob(childcare_tm_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lambda_tm)),
                            exits(glob(childcare_ck_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lambda_ck)))
)

           town pcfinhom_global_exits
1      Tampines                 FALSE
2 Choa Chu Kang                 FALSE


Neither town’s curve leaves the wider band either, as expected. The absence of residual interaction therefore does not depend on which envelope is used, unlike the J result above.
Neither r4gdsa chapter uses a non-cumulative function, so this correction is not available from them.


5.2.3.2 A null built from resident population
The inhomogeneous tests above have a circularity in them, which I set out in the section below: the intensity was estimated from a kernel density of the very points being tested, so genuine clustering could be absorbed into the “trend” before the test runs. Floch et al. say what the fix is, namely “a model that links a covariable to the intensity”. The covariable for childcare is obvious and I already have it, since Hands-on Exercise 1 used the same census table: resident children aged 0 to 4 by subzone.

pop_sz <- read_csv("../Hands-on_Ex01/data/aspatial/respop_census2020_agesex.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!grepl("Total", Number)) |>
  transmute(SUBZONE_N = toupper(Number),
            kids = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Total_0_4)))

mpsz_pop <- mpsz |>
  left_join(pop_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") |>
  mutate(kids = replace_na(kids, 0),
         kids_km2 = kids / as.numeric(st_area(mpsz) / 1e6))

c(subzone_polygons = nrow(mpsz_pop),
  name_found_in_census = sum(mpsz_pop$SUBZONE_N %in% pop_sz$SUBZONE_N),
  with_resident_count = sum(mpsz_pop$kids > 0),
  children_0_4 = sum(mpsz_pop$kids))

    subzone_polygons name_found_in_census  with_resident_count 
                 332                  332                  226 
        children_0_4 
              183100 


Every one of the 332 subzone names matches the census table, but only 226 carry a resident count. The other 106 are places like Raffles Place, Boat Quay, Jurong Island and the southern islands, where the census reports no resident population because nobody lives there. Those subzones should be zero, so this is not a gap in the join, and the total of 183,100 children agrees with the published national figure.
The next step turns this into a surface: rasterise the subzone densities, crop to the town, and scale the values so the surface integrates to the number of centres actually observed. That last step is what makes it a candidate intensity for the point process rather than just a population map.

kids_rast <- terra::rasterize(terra::vect(mpsz_pop),
                              terra::rast(terra::vect(mpsz_pop), resolution = 200),
                              field = "kids_km2")

pop_intensity <- function(town_sf, X) {
  rr  <- terra::crop(kids_rast, terra::vect(town_sf), mask = TRUE)
  mat <- terra::as.matrix(rr, wide = TRUE); mat[is.na(mat)] <- 0
  e   <- as.vector(terra::ext(rr))
  lam <- im(mat[nrow(mat):1, ], xrange = e[1:2] / 1000, yrange = e[3:4] / 1000)
  lam <- lam[Window(X), drop = FALSE]
  lam$v[is.na(lam$v) | lam$v <= 0] <- 1e-6
  lam$v <- lam$v * X$n / (sum(lam$v, na.rm = TRUE) * lam$xstep * lam$ystep)
  lam
}

lam_pop_tm <- pop_intensity(tm, childcare_tm_ppp_km)
lam_pop_ck <- pop_intensity(ck, childcare_ck_ppp_km)


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(lam_pop_tm, main = "Children 0-4 intensity: Tampines")
plot(lam_pop_ck, main = "Children 0-4 intensity: Choa Chu Kang")







par(mfrow = c(1, 1))


set.seed(42)
pcfpop_tm <- envelope(childcare_tm_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lam_pop_tm,
                    nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
pcfpop_ck <- envelope(childcare_ck_ppp_km, pcfinhom, lambda = lam_pop_ck,
                    nsim = 99, verbose = FALSE)
data.frame(
  town = c("Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang"),
  clustered = c(outside(pcfpop_tm, "above"), outside(pcfpop_ck, "above")),
  regular   = c(outside(pcfpop_tm, "below"), outside(pcfpop_ck, "below"))
)

           town  clustered regular
1      Tampines 0.01953125       0
2 Choa Chu Kang 0.00000000       0


The answer barely moves. Against a null built from where the children actually live, rather than from a smoothed version of the centres themselves, Choa Chu Kang shows nothing outside its envelope at any distance and Tampines shows a small excess over about 2% of the range.
The agreement is worth more than the size of the residual. The two nulls are built from completely different information, one from the childcare points and one from the census, and they point the same way. The circularity I was worried about does not appear to be driving the earlier result, and the conclusion now rests on an external covariate of the kind Floch et al. ask for rather than on the pattern explaining itself.
The small Tampines residual is the one thing I would look at next. It is weak enough to be noise across 99 simulations, but it is in the direction of clustering, and Tampines is the town where the housing is densest.


5.2.3.3 What none of this can settle
Section 4.3.2 of Floch et al., one of the core readings, is a warning that applies to everything above, and it is worth quoting because it states the problem more precisely than I could:

[T]he same aggregated or dispersed structures can be obtained with an inhomogeneous Poisson process in which the intensity of the process varies in space but the points are independent of each other. A single observation of a spatial distribution does not allow for any distinction between first- and second-order properties of a process in the absence of additional information such as that provided by a model that links a covariable to the intensity.

That is the identification problem this exercise ran into empirically. A clustered-looking map can mean centres attract each other (second-order), or that centres are simply more numerous where families live (first-order). One snapshot cannot separate them. Floch et al. cite Ellison and co-authors on exactly this: natural advantages, which raise intensity, have an effect “that is indistinguishable from that of positive externalities” causing aggregation. For childcare, “many young families here” and “operators cluster near each other” produce the same picture.
It also names the two standard escapes, and they are the two methods that appear in this exercise: the inhomogeneous K function of Baddeley et al., which I used through Linhom and pcfinhom, and the Kd of Duranton and Overman, which I did not.
This forces an honest qualification of my own result. The escape only works if the intensity comes from outside the pattern, from a covariate such as resident population. Mine did not. I estimated it with a kernel density of the very points being tested, so any genuine short-range clustering was partly absorbed into the “trend” before the test ran. That biases the inhomogeneous result towards finding nothing, which is what it found.
My conclusion is therefore narrower than it first appears. The pattern is consistent with centres being located wherever demand is, and this data cannot demonstrate interaction on top of that. That is not the same as proving no interaction exists.
Doing better needs the covariate, which is the natural next step and the reason the limitation below is first on the list.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
5.3 Limitations
Where this exercise falls short:

The population null is coarse. I did test against resident children aged 0 to 4 rather than only against CSR, which was the main gap. But the census gives one figure per subzone, so the intensity surface is a step function that jumps at subzone boundaries rather than a smooth demand surface. Any residual clustering measured at distances shorter than a subzone is partly a product of that blockiness.
Edge effects at the coast. All functions were used with their best available edge corrections, but the coastline makes the window irregular and some bias remains at short distances.
Description, not explanation. Even with the population covariate, this is still a description of where centres are. It says nothing about capacity, waiting lists or whether supply meets demand, and nothing about change over time. The spatio-temporal extension in Lesson 3 is where the time dimension starts.
Attribute data is thin. The current childcare table carries almost no useful attributes (capacity, hours, fees), so I could not stratify the analysis, e.g. cluster analysis for centres with and without infant-care places, which is the policy-relevant question.

None of these change the results above, but they do limit how far the results can be pushed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2
text:
5.4 Summary
At the national scale childcare supply is heavily concentrated, and the concentration sits in a central-eastern corridor that survives every bandwidth I tried. Clark-Evans, the quadrat chi-square test and the G, K and L functions all agree on that.
The second-order results need more care than the chapters suggest. Both towns look strongly clustered against a homogeneous CSR null, but that null assumes centres could have gone anywhere with equal probability, which is not true of a service that follows housing. Testing against an intensity-adjusted null instead, and using the non-cumulative pair correlation function rather than K or L, almost all of it goes. Choa Chu Kang shows no departure from its envelope at any distance, and Tampines only a small one, over about 2% of the range.
So the reading I would defend is that childcare centres are concentrated because people are concentrated, and that this data shows little sign of the centres responding to each other on top of that. That conclusion holds under both a pointwise and a global envelope, which is more than the J function manages.
Getting there took three corrections to my own first answer: one for the null, one for the cumulative functions, and one for reading pointwise bands as though they carried a significance level. None of the three would have surfaced from the chapters alone.

text:
This exercise applies Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis (STPPA) to forest fire detections in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia, during 2023. It follows r4gdsa Chapter 6, the chapter assigned for Lesson 3. Where I write “the chapter” below, I mean that one.
Lesson 2 treated a point pattern as a set of locations. A spatio-temporal point pattern adds the time of each event, so the same two questions from last week are asked again in three dimensions.
Part 1 reproduces Chapter 6. It has two halves: a first-order analysis of how fire intensity varies across space and time, using sparr, and a second-order analysis of whether events interact, using the space-time K-function in stpp. Part 2 examines the chapter’s method and adds one analysis it does not attempt.


The chapter asks:

Are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatial and spatio-temporally independent?
If the answer is no, where and when do the observed fire locations tend to cluster?

Independence is a second-order property, so the first question is addressed by the K-function in section 3.2. The second requires both halves: the density estimate locates the concentrations in space and time, and the K-function establishes whether they exceed what chance would produce.

text:
2.2 The data
Two datasets are needed: the fire detections and the boundary of the study area. The chapter names its sources but distributes neither file, so both were retrieved directly.

2.2.1 Fire detections
The chapter uses forestfires.csv, described as MODIS detections from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System. The download page it links requires an account and delivers the file by email. The same archive is also published as a direct download with no account, one file per country per year:
https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/data/country/modis/2023/modis_2023_Indonesia.csv
That is the file used here. It holds every MODIS detection in Indonesia for 2023 and is kept whole, so the cut to Bangka is done in the code below and stays visible.


2.2.2 Study area boundary
The chapter reads an ESRI shapefile named Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung, extracted from a national file on the Indonesia Geospatial portal. That portal distributes its files through a blog page linking to Google Drive, so there is no stable URL to cite.
I used GADM instead, level 2, which is the regency and city level (kabupaten and kota):
https://geodata.ucdavis.edu/gadm/gadm4.1/json/gadm41_IDN_2.json.zip
The chapter’s file is at kelurahan level, one step finer, but the chapter immediately dissolves it with st_union(), so the boundary that reaches the analysis is identical either way. Level 2 also keeps the regencies available, which is the administrative unit required for Take-home Exercise 1.


2.2.3 Coordinate reference system
Everything is transformed to EPSG:32748, WGS 84 / UTM zone 48S, which is the projected system the chapter uses and the correct UTM zone for Bangka Belitung. Units are metres, so every bandwidth and distance below reads in metres.

3.1 The study area
GADM ships the whole country, so the province is selected by name and then dissolved into a single polygon. st_zm() drops the Z dimension, which as.owin() will not accept, and the transform puts the result in metres.

kbb_full <- st_read("data/rawdata/gadm41_IDN_2.json", quiet = TRUE) |>
  filter(NAME_1 == "BangkaBelitung") |>
  st_union() |>
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") |>
  st_transform(crs = 32748)

GADM maps every offshore rock as its own polygon, so this boundary arrives in 270 separate pieces. Most of them are far too small to carry a forest fire.

parts <- st_cast(kbb_full, "POLYGON", warn = FALSE)
part_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(parts)) / 1e6

c(parts = length(parts),
  largest_km2 = round(max(part_km2), 1),
  smallest_km2 = round(min(part_km2), 4))

       parts  largest_km2 smallest_km2 
    270.0000   11602.5000       0.0001 


The two main islands account for 11,603 km² and 4,617 km², which is 97% of the total. The smallest pieces are a few hundredths of a square kilometre. Fires cannot occur on those, and a window made of 270 fragments makes the density estimate slower without changing it, so anything under 1 km² is dropped.

kbb_sf <- st_union(parts[part_km2 >= 1])

  area_km2 = round(as.numeric(st_area(kbb_sf)) / 1e6, 1),
  pct_of_original = round(100 * as.numeric(st_area(kbb_sf)) /
                            as.numeric(st_area(kbb_full)), 2))

4.2 Computing the K-function

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)

The chapter’s next step is plotK(kbb_stik). That call produces nothing inside a Quarto document, and it fails silently rather than raising an error. Its first act is to inspect the open graphics devices and, if it finds one, close it and open a new one:
devl = dev.list()
if (is.null(devl)) { ... } else {
    dev.off(devl[length(devl)])
    dev.new()
Under Quarto a device is always already open, the one knitr is writing the figure file to. So plotK() closes it, draws onto a fresh device that nothing is capturing, and the chunk finishes with no image and no warning.

plotK(kbb_stik)

Everything after those first lines is ordinary base graphics on the object STIKhat() returns, so the same surface can be drawn directly. Khat holds the estimate and Ktheo the value expected under space-time independence, so the difference is what carries the signal, which is what plotK(L = TRUE) would show.

k_diff <- kbb_stik$Khat - kbb_stik$Ktheo
lv <- pretty(c(-max(abs(k_diff)), max(abs(k_diff))), n = 15)

filled.contour(x = kbb_stik$dist,
               y = kbb_stik$times,
               z = k_diff,
               levels = lv,
               color.palette = colorRampPalette(c("red", "white", "blue")),
               xlab = "spatial distance u (metres)",
               ylab = "time lag v (days)",
               main = expression(hat(K)[ST](u, v) - K[theo]))

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
4.3 Reading the plot
Blue is positive, meaning more pairs of fires at that combination of distance and time lag than space-time independence would produce. Red would be fewer. The whole surface here is positive, and it rises steadily along both axes, reaching about 4.9 x 10^12 at the far corner.
Read across the bottom, at short time lags, the excess grows with distance, which says fires on nearby days are spread across the island rather than confined to one spot. Read up the right, at large distances, the excess grows with time lag as well. The two together describe a pattern that is clustered in space and time jointly: the fire season concentrates events into part of the year, and within that period they appear across a wide area at once.
The estimate is computed over spatial distances from 3.2 km to 47.6 km and time lags from 6 to 89 days, which STIKhat() chose from the data.
Two limits on this reading. STIKhat() was called without a lambda argument, so it uses its own internal intensity estimate as the reference; a different intensity model would move the surface. And there is no envelope here, so nothing on this plot says whether the excess is larger than sampling variation would produce. Part 3 takes both of those up.
